lesson.subtitle: Lesson 8 -- What the Speakers Said
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Juliane Albieri Calixto | Lesson 8 -- What the Speakers Said
lesson.grammar_point: reported speech: said that, told us that, explained that, with the verb one step back in time

listenings.text: Good morning, everybody. I want to start with a confession. For years, my team designed for a perfect user. A user with time, a new phone and a good connection. But that user doesn't exist. Real users are tired. They are busy. They are on a bus, with a bad connection and a baby on their lap. So today I have one message: design for the worst day of your user, not for the best one. And I'll tell you what we will do next year. We will test every feature with users on their worst day: late at night, in a hurry, with a slow phone. If it works then, it will work always.

Hi Juliane, it's Daniel. I'm calling from Chicago. I just came back from a conference, and I thought of you, because the best talk was about banks. The speaker was a designer from a bank in Singapore. She said that most bank apps were designed for experts, not for normal people. She told us that the words on the screens were the biggest problem, not the design. And she gave us a simple exercise. She told the audience to read their app out loud to a person who is not a designer. If the person didn't understand, the text was wrong. I think your team would love that idea. I'll send you the video.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: an important idea you remember and use after a talk
to say something quickly, without many details
the results of research or a study
a short text with the main ideas of something longer
the main talk at a conference
to show that something is important
how easy it is for everybody to use a product
a change or a new direction that many people follow

paras: Last week I went to a design conference in Amsterdam, and I promised my team a short summary. The keynote speaker was the head of design of a big travel app. She said that most product teams were still designing for the perfect user, and that real users were tired, busy and distracted. Her main takeaway: design for the worst day of your user, not for the best one.

The second talk was about accessibility. The speaker highlighted some findings from his research: when his team made their app easier for blind users, it also became faster for everybody. He told us that accessibility was not a feature, but a quality of every feature. He also mentioned a free tool to check the contrast of the colors, but he didn’t explain how to use it.

The last talk was about AI. The speaker explained that AI would change the work of designers, but it wouldn’t replace them. She said the trend was clear: in two years, every designer would use AI every day, so the important skill would be to ask good questions. I want to share these three ideas with you in our next team meeting.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- B1 reading, written for this lesson as a model of a conference report
